- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecast overshoot, reduce peak values by 5–10% to account for mean reversion or policy-induced volatility.
- In periods with high sentiment (≥0.7), model often underestimates upward momentum; increase forecast mid-range by 2–5% to capture bullish sentiment-driven rally.
- If true outcome shows strong downward trend after a high peak, model frequently fails to recognize the turn; add a 3–5 day lagged smoothing filter to dampen over-optimistic peaks.
- When sentiment drops sharply after a peak, model often fails to anticipate the correction; apply a “sentiment decay” multiplier (e.g., 0.85–0.9) to forecast values in the 2–5 day window post-sentiment drop.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overestimate volatility in early days; cap forecast variance within 10% of 14-day moving average to avoid over-shock responses.
